canonical_title: The Mainstream That Through the Ghetto Flows: An Interview with Philip K. Dick
author: Philip K. Dick (interviewee)
card_summary: A substantial late interview published in The Missouri Review in 1984, in which PKD talks at length about the divide between literary fiction and the science-fiction ghetto, his abandoned mainstream novels, and his own place between the two.
page_summary:
Published in The Missouri Review in 1984, two years after PKD's death, this long interview takes its title from his lifelong preoccupation: the border between respectable literary fiction, the mainstream, and the low-status science-fiction ghetto in which he made his career. PKD had spent the 1950s writing realist novels that publishers rejected, and the wound of that failure, alongside his pride in what science fiction could do, runs through the conversation.

Over its length the interview ranges across his working life, his sense of the genre, the mainstream books that went unpublished until late, and his understanding of himself as a writer who never fully belonged to either camp. It is one of the fuller late statements of how PKD saw his own literary standing.

As a posthumously published interview it is a primary source for PKD's views on his career and on the literary hierarchy that shaped it, in his own recorded words.
